name: Lumun
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source.
catalog_citation: Smits, Heleen (2017). A grammar of Lumun: a Kordofanian language of Sudan. PhD dissertation, Leiden University. Utrecht: LOT (LOT 465).https://www.lotpublications.nl/Documents/465_fulltext.pdf
catalog_locator: ch. 3 Tone, §3.1.1 'Four tonemes', pp. 81-82; §3.1.2 (mora as TBU) pp. 83-84; ch. 4 §4.2 'Tone patterns' pp. 123-124 (Arabic loans)
catalog_quote: Lumun can be analysed as having four tonemes: high (H), low (L), falling (HL) and rising (LH). These tones are contrastive in prepausal positions, cf. the following words. Low tone is unmarked. ... L vs. H kərək 'farming field' kərə́k 'bellies' ... The oppositions show that it is useful to take the mora, not the syllable as the unit on which a toneme —low, high, rising or falling— is realized. ... Originally Lumun nouns with more than one vowel do not have a high tone on the first vowel. ... An initial high tone on a simple noun with more than one vowel is found in several Arabic loans. The tone mimics the stress placement in the Arabic item. Some examples: páka 'jerrycan' (< Sudanese Arabic baagha) mʊ́ccʊt̪ 'comb' (< Sudanese Arabic mushuṭ) cɛ́rət̪ɛl 'bucket' (< Sudanese Arabic jerdal)

tone_statements.citation: Norton, Russell. 2018. Parallel Grammar Documentation in Four Talodi Languages. Afrikanistik-Aegyptologie-Online 2018: 1-34. doi:10.18716/ojs/aaeo/2018_3457 (urn:nbn:de:0009-10-48877).
tone_statements.quote: Tone presents a more serious problem: since tone is not marked in the orthographies of the languages in this survey, tone is also absent from the phonetic re-transcriptions of the writers’ data in this survey. Talodi languages appear to fit a type of African language in which tone has a low functional load in the lexicon, where the case for exhaustively representing tone in the orthography is unpersuasive (Kutsch Lojenga 2014a:63). ... However, tone is known to have a role in forming imperative verbs in both Lumun and Dagik (Smits 2017:339-341, Vanderelst 2016:108)

audit.reasoning: The classification 'tonal' rests on the standard and only reference grammar of Lumun (Smits 2017, 777 pp.), which we hold; the deciding quotation was confirmed verbatim at the stated pages (81, 83, 123). The grammar devotes a full chapter to tone and never describes word stress; its sole use of 'stress' refers to Arabic source words. Glottolog lists no competing grammar or phonology (the one 'phonology' entry is an 8-page orthography note; earlier phonology sketches are unpublished typescripts cited by Smits). the one works still to obtain is a comparative Talodi paper of low priority that would at most add an explicit 'no stress' remark.

sources.quote: Tone presents a more serious problem: since tone is not marked in the orthographies of the languages in this survey, tone is also absent from the phonetic re-transcriptions of the writers’ data in this survey. Talodi languages appear to fit a type of African language in which tone has a low functional load in the lexicon, where the case for exhaustively representing tone in the orthography is unpersuasive (Kutsch Lojenga 2014a:63). ... However, tone is known to have a role in forming imperative verbs in both Lumun and Dagik (Smits 2017:339-341, Vanderelst 2016:108)
sources.note: Not a tone study. States that tone is unmarked in the Talodi orthographies and therefore absent from his re-transcriptions; characterises Talodi languages as a type in which tone has a low functional load in the lexicon; notes grammatical tone: imperative verbs are formed with tone in Lumun (citing Smits 2017:339-341) and Dagik, so imperative tone is reconstructed to Proto-Talodi; flags Lumun homograph pronouns where 'a difference in tone was heard' (para <47>, p. 22). No tone inventory given; does not contradict Smits's four-toneme analysis.
